السوداني والدعم السريع , الخرطوم , السودان , الطاقة , النيل الأبيض , نهر النيل 0 محطة كهرباء شندي التحويلية خرجت من الخدمة بصورة كاملة شندي، 30 أكتوبر 2026 – قصفت مسيّرات للدعم السريع، الجمعة، مقار عسكرية للجيش ومحطة الكهرباء التحويلية في مدينة شندي بولاية نهر النيل، شمالي السودان، ضمن سلسلة هجمات طالت محطات الكهرباء ومخزونات الوقود. وقالت اللجنة الأمنية لمحلية شندي بولاية نهر في بيان أن محطة كهرباء شندي التحويلية خرجت من الخدمة بصورة كاملة بعد الدمار الذي طال المحولات جراء قصفها بمسيرة صباح اليوم. وأفادت اللجنة لدى تفقدها الأضرار بالمحطة التحويلية أن قصف المسيرات طال أيضا مستودع احتياطي للوقود لشركة النيل ومبنى يتبع للدفاع الجوي. وخلال أقل من أسبوعين استهدفت مسيّرات انقضاضية واستراتيجية لقوات الدعم السريع 11 محطة كهرباء ومحطات وقود في 7 ولايات على الأقل. واتهمت الحكومة السودانية إثيوبيا بالتورط في قصف محطات الكهرباء عبر مسيّرات قالت إنها انطلقت من إثيوبيا، عوضاً عن الدعم الإثيوبي لقوات الدعم السريع. وطبقاً لمصادر محلية تحدثت لـ«سودان تربيون»، فإن مسيّرات هاجمت عند حوالي الساعة 02:40 من صباح اليوم الجمعة مدينة شندي، نحو 160 كيلومتراً شمالي العاصمة الخرطوم. وأفادت المصادر بأن الهجوم بالطيران المسيّر أسفر عن استهداف محطة كهرباء شندي التحويلية، مما تسبب في اشتعال حريق بالمحطة، مما تسبب في انقطاع التيار الكهربائي عن مدينة شندي وضواحيها بالتزامن مع سماع دوي عدة انفجارات. كما هاجمت مسيّرات الدعم السريع مقار عسكرية بمدينة شندي، شملت مقر الفرقة الثالثة مشاة التابعة للجيش ومستودعاً للوقود، بينما تصدت الدفاعات الأرضية للجيش للمسيّرات الانتحارية وأحبطت هجومها. وكانت مسيّرات الدعم السريع قد هاجمت محطة كهرباء أم دباكر، وهي أكبر محطة حرارية بالبلاد، في مدينة ربك بولاية النيل الأبيض صباح أمس، مما أدى إلى إصابة 4 محولات فضلاً عن أضرار لحقت بوحدة المعالجة، وهو ما أخرج المحطة عن الخدمة. الكلمات: شندي، نهر النيل، محطة كهرباء شندي، مسيّرات الدعم السريع، انقطاع الكهرباء، أم دباكر، الفرقة الثالثة مشاة، إثيوبيا، منشآت الطاقة، الحرب في السودان مقالات ذات صلة تحالف سوداني مؤيد للجيش يبحث مسار التحول لحكم ديمقراطي (إيقاد) تُوصي الاتحاد الأفريقي بتعيين مبعوث خاص أكثر من 400 مدني و102 من العسكريين. ولم يتم التحقق من هذه الادعاءات بشكل مستقل. عرض مسؤولون سودانيون هذه الاتهامات خلال إحاطة حضرها كبار المسؤولين العسكريين والاستخباراتيين ووكلاء وزارتي الخارجية والإعلام. وسمّوا الدمازين والمزموم وسنار وكوستي وربك وبلونق والكرمك والدندر وود الماحي والأبيض وأبو عوييلة وبارة وأم روابة كأهداف مزعومة. وقال المسؤولون إن عشرات المدارس ومحطات الوقود والمراكز الصحية والمستشفيات دُمّرت. وزعموا أن الطائرات المسيّرة أُطلقت من قواعد في أسوسا وبحر دار ومواقع على طول الحدود السودانية، وأن مسارات طيرانها امتدت بمحاذاة جنوب السودان. وأضافوا أن الطائرات شملت مسيّرات انتحارية معدّلة وبعيدة المدى، بما في ذلك طرازات صينية الصنع ومسيّرات بيرقدار أقينجي وبيرقدار تي بي 2 تركية الصنع. وقال المسؤولون أيضاً إن القوات السودانية أسقطت عدة طائرات مسيّرة، بينها طرازات أقينجي وCH-95. وقال وكيل وزارة الخارجية معاوية عثمان خالد إن السودان ينتهج «الصبر الاستراتيجي»، مع تأكيده أنه سيدافع عن سيادته ووحدة أراضيه. ودعا إلى تحرك دولي بشأن ما وصفه بأنه عدوان يهدد المدنيين والاستقرار الإقليمي. وقال المشاركون في الإحاطة إن الضربات تهدف إلى منع النازحين، ولا سيما الموجودين في الخرطوم، من العودة إلى ديارهم، وإلى تقويض الجهود الرامية لاستعادة الحياة الطبيعية. وكانت إثيوبيا قد رفضت سابقاً اتهامات بدعمها لقوات الدعم السريع، ووصفتها بأنها لا أساس لها. وفي سياق منفصل، قال وزير الدفاع حسن داود كبرون إن أكثر من 20 دولة متورطة في الحرب عبر الدعم اللوجستي والمرتزقة والتمويل بحري من ساحل مسندم ترامب عن حرب إيران: ستنتهي قريبا    E ع   السودان يعزز الإجراءات الأمنية لحماية الشاحنات المصرية قيادة قوات الحرس الوطني السوداني 'درع الشمال' ستعمل على تأمين الشاحنات المصرية وحمولاتها وسائقيها على طريق الصادرات الشمالي، انطلاقا من المعبر الحدودي وصولا إلى نهاية الولاية الشمالية. الجمعة 2026/10/30 الجيش السوداني يسعى لاحتواء أزمة مع القاهرة بعد مقتل سائقين مصريين الخرطوم - تعهدت قوات سودانية بتوفير حماية أمنية مشددة للشاحنات المصرية على الطرق التجارية، في مسعى لاحتواء تداعيات مقتل سائقين مصريين بالرصاص في العاصمة الخرطوم، والحيلولة دون اتساع التوتر بين البلدين، بعدما تزامن الهجوم مع غضب سوداني إثر غارة جوية استهدفت عمالا في مواقع للتنقيب عن المعادن قرب الحدود المصرية. وأعلنت قيادة قوات الحرس الوطني السوداني "درع الشمال"، عبر إدارة التأمين وحماية الطرق القومية، استعدادها لتأمين الشاحنات المصرية وحمولاتها وسائقيها على طريق الصادرات الشمالي، انطلاقا من المعبر الحدودي وصولا إلى نهاية الولاية الشمالية. وقالت إنها نشرت دوريات ثابتة ومتحركة وقوات للتدخل السريع، إلى جانب غرفة عمليات تعمل على مدار الساعة لمتابعة حركة النقل والاستجابة للبلاغات الطارئة. ودعت القوات السائقين إلى التقيد بتوجيهات العناصر المنتشرة عند نقاط التفتيش، والتواصل مع غرفة العمليات عند مواجهة أي طارئ، مؤكدة أن هذه التدابير تستهدف ضمان سلامة العابرين واستئناف حركة النقل البري التي تعطلت عقب الحادث. وكان مسلح قد أطلق النار في 12 أكتوبر/تشرين الأول على مجموعة من سائقي الشاحنات المصريين في سوق جنوبي الخرطوم، ما أدى إلى مقتل اثنين وإصابة ثالث. وأعلنت القاهرة أن السلطات السودانية ألقت القبض على المشتبه به، فيما أفادت تقارير إعلامية بأنه قال إن إطلاق النار جاء انتقاما لمقتل شقيقه في الغارة الجوية التي استهدفت مواقع للتعدين شمالي السودان، وهي رواية لم تتضح جميع ملابساتها بصورة مستقلة. وسبق الحادث بأيام استهداف جوي لمواقع تنقيب أهلي عن الذهب في منطقة جبل العقيْدات بولاية البحر الأحمر، قرب الحدود مع مصر. واتهمت منظمة "محامو الطوارئ" الجيش المصري بتنفيذ الضربات، وقالت إنها أوقعت 72 قتيلا على الأقل، بينما تحدث ناجون لوسائل إعلام سودانية عن حصيلة تجاوزت 200 قتيل. ولم يتسن التحقق بصورة مستقلة من هذه الأرقام أو تحديد الجهة المسؤولة عن الهجوم، في حين أعلن الجيش المصري تنفيذ عمليات ضد أنشطة التعدين غير القانوني داخل الأراضي المصرية، من دون إقرار بمسؤوليته عن الغارة. وأمر رئيس مجلس السيادة السوداني الفريق اول عبدالفتاح البرهان بتشكيل لجنة لتقصي الحقائق بشأن الضربات، تضم ممثلين عن النيابة العامة والجهات القضائية والأمنية، فيما أكدت الخرطوم والقاهرة استمرار التواصل لكشف ملابسات الحوادث والحفاظ على العلاقات الثنائية. وفي المقابل، أوقفت السلطات المصرية في 16 أكتوبر/تشرين الاول عبور الشاحنات المتجهة إلى السودان عبر ميناء قسطل البري، المقابل لميناء أشكيت، إلى حين صدور تعليمات جديدة، مع استمرار السماح بعبور المسافرين والمركبات غير التجارية. ويعكس التعهد السوداني بتأمين الناقلات محاولة لإعادة الثقة في المسار التجاري ومنع تحول الاعتداءات الفردية إلى أزمة أوسع. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Su-35 Fighter Jets, to Receive S-400 Air Defense Systems: PM Abiy - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Su-35 Fighter Jets, to Receive S-400 Air Defense Systems: PM Abiy - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Su-35 Fighter Jets, to Receive S-400 Air Defense Systems: PM Abiy 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, October 28, 2026 (ENA)— Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has announced that the country has taken delivery of its first 12 Su-35 4++ generation fighter jets and is set to receive four batteries of S-400 air defense systems. The Prime Minister described the move as a significant milestone in Ethiopia’s efforts to strengthen its national defense and security capabilities. In a social media post, PM Abiy said Ethiopia’s comprehensive efforts to sustainably ensure peace and security had reached a new milestone. He added that the growing readiness of the country’s defense forces was enhancing its ability to deter potential aggression. “Today, in accordance with our prior agreement with the Russian government, we have taken delivery of the first twelve Su-35 4++ Generation fighter jets,” he said, adding that Ethiopia would also receive four S-400 air defense system batteries. Prime Minister Abiy expressed gratitude to Russian President Vladimir Putin for facilitating the delivery of the fighter jets a year ahead of the agreed schedule. He said the acquisition places Ethiopia at the forefront of Sub-Saharan African nations in equipping itself with the advanced fighter jets. The Prime Minister further elaborated that the development further strengthens Ethiopia’s sovereignty and enhances its defense capabilities, enabling the country to pursue its national security objectives while contributing to regional stability. The announcement comes as Prime Minister Abiy arrives in Moscow, Russia, to attend the Third Russia–Africa Summit, providing an opportunity to advance Ethiopia’s engagement with Russia and other African nations. The Prime Minister described the acquisition as a significant boost to Ethiopia’s collective security and its long-term efforts to safeguard national sovereignty and regional peace. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

ethiopia.title: Fading Hopes, Rising Needs - Renewed Fighting Threatens Another Humanitarian Catastrophe in Tigray
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Fading Hopes, Rising Needs - Renewed Fighting Threatens Another Humanitarian Catastrophe in Tigray - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Fading Hopes, Rising Needs - Renewed Fighting Threatens Another Humanitarian Catastrophe in Tigray 30 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Renewed fighting in Tigray, northern Ethiopia, is pushing an already vulnerable population towards another humanitarian catastrophe. Nearly four years after the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement was signed to end the devastating war between the Ethiopian federal government and Tigrayan forces, renewed hostilities have raised serious concerns about civilian safety, mass displacement, food insecurity, and the disruption of essential services. For millions of people in Tigray, the consequences of the previous war have never truly ended. Families continue to struggle with displacement, hunger, damaged health facilities, destroyed livelihoods, and the loss of loved ones. The renewed violence threatens to reverse the limited progress made towards recovery and deepen the suffering of communities that have endured years of conflict. The severity of the crisis is evident not only in reports of casualties, growing humanitarian needs, and continuing displacement, but also in the experiences of people struggling to survive in displacement centers. Their testimonies reveal the human consequences of a crisis that extends far beyond the battlefield. This is not simply another security crisis. It is a humanitarian emergency unfolding in a region where communities' capacity to withstand another war has already been severely weakened. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Fragile healthcare system, deepening civilian suffering The resumption of hostilities in late September 2026 has intensified fears for civilians across Tigray. Reports from humanitarian organizations indicate that renewed fighting, drone strikes, and insecurity have placed civilians at greater risk while disrupting healthcare and other essential services. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) reported a sharp increase in war-wounded patients at hospitals in northern Ethiopia during the first days of renewed fighting. At facilities in Korem and Alamata, the number of wounded patients rose from approximately 180 over 48 hours to more than 420 between 22 and 25 September. Suhul Hospital in Shire also received more than 300 war-wounded patients by 25 September . These figures illustrate the immediate human cost of renewed hostilities and the pressure placed on an already fragile healthcare system. Medical teams must respond to growing emergency needs while insecurity restricts movement and makes it increasingly difficult to deliver assistance. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has also warned that renewed hostilities are heightening humanitarian concerns in northern Ethiopia. Although its teams have delivered medical supplies to health facilities across Tigray, continuing insecurity threatens civilians' access to treatment, food, clean water, electricity, and other necessities. For people who already face limited access to healthcare, renewed fighting presents an additional threat. Injured civilians may struggle to reach hospitals, while patients with chronic illnesses risk losing access to regular treatment. Disrupted electricity, shortages of medical supplies, and restrictions on movement can further undermine the ability of healthcare facilities to provide essential services. Protecting civilians must come before military objectives. Humanitarian access must come before political calculations." Behind every casualty figure is a person, a family, and a community facing uncertainty about survival. The growing pressure on hospitals is therefore not merely a question of medical capacity; it is a warning of the wider humanitarian consequences of renewed conflict. No safe place to return One of the most serious consequences of renewed fighting is the risk of further displacement. Thousands of families who have already experienced displacement may once again be forced to abandon their homes in search of safety. For many, however, leaving home does not guarantee protection. Displaced people may face shortages of food, shelter, clean water, medical care, and other essential supplies. The situation is particularly concerning for people displaced during the previous war who have been unable to return to their places of origin. Hundreds of thousands of people displaced from Western Tigray remain unable to return home, leaving families separated from their communities, land, property, and livelihoods. Renewed fighting threatens to compound their suffering by creating additional displacement while placing further pressure on the limited resources available to support existing displaced populations. The human cost of this prolonged displacement becomes clearer when the experiences of individual families are considered. In September 2026, I travelled to an internally displaced persons (IDP) centre in Mekelle as a research assistant, where I interviewed displaced families about their experiences and the hardships they continue to face. Among those I met was Senait Gebrekidan, who had been displaced from Humera, in Western Tigray. Senait described the dire living conditions facing displaced families, explaining that many were struggling to secure enough food to eat. According to her testimony, the 15-kilogram food ration that families were supposed to receive was frequently delayed. Essential items such as clothing, cooking oil, and medicine had become luxuries that many could no longer afford. She also reported that the last food distribution at the center had taken place in June, leaving families struggling to survive without regular assistance. Reports on IDP conditions in Tigray have repeatedly highlighted critical malnutrition and severe medicine shortages stemming from gaps in aid distribution. Her account illustrates how displacement can become a prolonged struggle for survival rather than a temporary escape from violence. For families such as Senait's, the absence of regular food assistance means that even the most necessities cannot be taken for granted. The hardship is especially severe for children, older people, pregnant women, people with disabilities, and individuals who require continuous medical treatment. Families forced to flee may lose access to education, healthcare, employment, and the social networks that once helped them cope with difficult circumstances. For displaced people, the crisis is not measured only by the distance they travel to escape violence. It is also measured by the length of time they remain without a safe home, adequate assistance, or a realistic prospect of rebuilding their lives. Senait's experience raises urgent questions about the adequacy and continuity of humanitarian assistance in displacement centers. When food distributions are delayed or interrupted, families already deprived of their homes and livelihoods are left with even fewer options for survival. Humanitarian organizations, government authorities, and international partners must ensure that displaced people receive regular assistance and adequate protection, regardless of where they originate or which areas they have been forced to leave. Fighting returns, hunger deepens Renewed fighting is unfolding amid an already severe food crisis. According to reporting on a September 2026 assessment by the Tigray Disaster Risk Management Commission, approximately 3.9 million people in the region require emergency food assistance . This situation has been aggravated by disrupted agricultural production, poor rainfall, inaccessible farmland, and the continuing consequences of years of conflict. Agriculture remains a principal source of livelihood for many households. Yet insecurity, displacement, damaged infrastructure, and limited access to farmland have undermined families' ability to produce sufficient food or earn an income. Renewed hostilities threaten to make matters worse by disrupting transportation, market activity, fuel supplies, and access to agricultural land. Farmers who cannot safely reach their fields may lose critical harvesting opportunities, while traders may struggle to transport food into affected communities. For displaced households, the consequences are particularly severe. Many have lost access to their land, livestock, and other productive assets. Without reliable humanitarian assistance or opportunities to earn an income, families may be unable to meet their basic nutritional needs. Senait's testimony provides a concrete example of this wider problem. The reported delays in food distributions at the Mekelle IDP center demonstrate how interruptions in assistance can leave already vulnerable families struggling to obtain even basic food supplies. The consequences extend beyond immediate hunger. Prolonged food shortages can lead to malnutrition, deteriorating health , interruptions to children's education, and the sale of essential household assets to survive. Children and people with existing health conditions are particularly vulnerable to the effects of inadequate nutrition. Humanitarian assistance must reach vulnerable communities before these pressures become even more severe. Regular emergency food distributions, nutrition programs, clean water, and healthcare support are essential to preventing further suffering. The reported food shortages in displacement centers also underscore the importance of monitoring humanitarian assistance to ensure that promised distributions are delivered consistently and that gaps are addressed before they become life-threatening. Humanitarian access under threat The ability of humanitarian organizations to respond effectively is another major concern. Insecurity can prevent aid workers from reaching affected communities, delay medical evacuations, interrupt the movement of relief supplies, and restrict the collection of reliable information about civilian needs. When fighting blocks humanitarian access , humanitarian agencies struggle to deliver food, medicine, and fuel where assistance is most urgently required. These obstacles are especially dangerous in a region where millions of people already depend on humanitarian support. The reported difficulties faced by displaced families illustrate why the continuity of humanitarian assistance is essential. When food distributions are interrupted, families who have lost their homes and livelihoods may have no alternative source of support. For those who depend on humanitarian aid for their daily survival, even a prolonged delay can have serious consequences. The international community must recognize that humanitarian access is not a secondary consideration to be addressed after military operations. It is an immediate necessity. All parties to the conflict must allow and facilitate rapid, safe, and unhindered humanitarian assistance to civilians in need. Humanitarian personnel, medical facilities, ambulances, relief convoys, and essential civilian infrastructure must be protected. The destruction, looting, or obstruction of facilities used to coordinate humanitarian assistance can have consequences far beyond the immediate damage. It can deprive entire communities of food, medicine, shelter, and other life-saving resources. Humanitarian organizations must also be able to assess needs independently and communicate their findings without intimidation or political interference. Beyond allowing aid to enter affected areas, humanitarian actors and relevant authorities must ensure that assistance reaches the people for whom it is intended. Displaced families need predictable, adequate, and continuous support, particularly where prolonged displacement has left them with few means of survival. Without safe access, reliable needs assessments, and sustained assistance, humanitarian organizations will struggle to respond to the growing demands of a population already weakened by years of conflict. From diplomatic statements to concrete action The international community cannot afford to treat renewed fighting in Tigray as another temporary security crisis. Years of violence have demonstrated the devastating consequences of delayed responses, inadequate civilian protection, and political agreements that fail to deliver lasting security. Statements expressing concern are important, but they are not enough. Civilians need practical measures that reduce the risk of further deaths, protect displaced families, and ensure that humanitarian assistance reaches those who need it. The United Nations, the African Union, the European Union, regional governments, and international humanitarian organizations should urgently coordinate efforts to implement the following measures. First, protect civilians . All parties must comply with international humanitarian law, distinguish between civilians and combatants, and take every feasible precaution to prevent civilian deaths and injuries. Attacks directed against civilians and civilian objects are prohibited. Second, secure humanitarian access . Safe and unhindered routes must be established for humanitarian convoys, medical teams, and emergency supplies. Communications and essential services should be restored wherever they have been disrupted. Third, expand emergency assistance . Food, clean water, shelter, medical supplies, and nutritional support must be prioritized for displaced people and communities facing acute shortages. Humanitarian partners should also assess the adequacy and regularity of food distributions in IDP centres to identify and address gaps in assistance. Fourth, strengthen independent monitoring . International and independent humanitarian and human rights organizations should have access to affected areas to assess civilian harm, investigate credible allegations of abuses, and document displacement and humanitarian needs. Fifth, protect displaced people's rights . Displaced families must not be forced to return to unsafe areas. Any return must be voluntary, safe, and dignified, with meaningful access to housing, land, property, essential services, and livelihoods. Sixth, intensify diplomatic efforts . Regional and international actors should press all parties to halt the escalation, return to a credible political process, and implement outstanding commitments under the Pretoria peace agreement. These measures should not depend on the political identity, ethnicity, or geographical location of the people affected. Humanitarian assistance must be provided according to need, and civilian protection must remain an obligation for all parties. International engagement must also extend beyond statements and emergency appeals. Diplomatic pressure, independent monitoring, and sustained engagement are necessary to prevent further escalation and ensure that commitments to peace translate into meaningful improvements in people's lives. Beyond emergency aid Emergency assistance can save lives, but it cannot independently resolve the underlying causes of the humanitarian crisis . A lasting solution requires more than temporary shelter and food distributions. It requires security, accountability, political dialogue, restored public services, and conditions that allow displaced people to rebuild their lives. The continued displacement of people from Western Tigray is a reminder that the consequences of the previous war remain unresolved. Sustainable solutions must address civilian protection, access to homes and property, and the rights of people who have been unable to return to their places of origin. For displaced families, a lasting solution means more than receiving food and shelter in temporary accommodation. It means having a realistic opportunity to return voluntarily to a safe environment, recover their livelihoods, reunite with their communities, and rebuild their lives with dignity. The people of Tigray should not have to endure another cycle of violence before the world responds with urgency." Until these conditions are established, many families will remain dependent on humanitarian assistance, exposed to insecurity, and uncertain about their future. The international community must also recognize that peace agreements cannot succeed through signatures alone. Their implementation must produce tangible improvements in the lives of ordinary people. The Pretoria agreement was intended to end a devastating war and create conditions for peace. Renewed fighting highlights the urgency of addressing outstanding political and security challenges through dialogue and implementation of the agreement's commitments. Without meaningful progress towards civilian protection, safe return, accountability, and political reconciliation, renewed fighting risks perpetuating a cycle in which each new escalation creates further displacement and deepens existing humanitarian needs. A sustainable response must therefore combine immediate humanitarian relief with long-term efforts to address insecurity, protect rights, restore essential services, and establish conditions for lasting peace. Conclusion: For Tigray's civilians, survival cannot wait Tigray stands at a dangerous crossroads. Renewed fighting threatens to deepen an already devastating humanitarian crisis, putting civilians at risk of death, displacement, hunger, and the loss of essential services. For families still struggling to recover from the previous war, another escalation represents not merely a political or military development but a renewed threat to their survival. The testimony of Senait Gebrekidan, a displaced woman from Humera whom I interviewed at an IDP centre in Mekelle, illustrates the daily hardships facing families who remain uprooted from their homes. Her account of delayed food distributions and the lack of access to essential items highlights the urgent need for reliable humanitarian assistance. Behind the wider figures on displacement and food insecurity are people trying to survive under conditions that no family should have to endure. Their suffering must not become normalized, and their needs must not be overlooked because the crisis has persisted for years. The international community must act before the situation deteriorates further. Humanitarian organizations need access, displaced families need protection, hospitals need supplies, and civilians need safety. The people of Tigray should not have to endure another cycle of violence before the world responds with urgency. Protecting civilians must come before military objectives. Humanitarian access must come before political calculations. And lasting peace must be measured by whether ordinary people can live safely in their homes, feed their families, access healthcare, and rebuild their futures. The time for urgent and coordinated humanitarian action is now. ethiopia.title: As Tens of Thousands Flee Ethiopia to Kenya, UN Agency Warns of Growing Humanitarian Needs
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: As Tens of Thousands Flee Ethiopia to Kenya, UN Agency Warns of Growing Humanitarian Needs - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: As Tens of Thousands Flee Ethiopia to Kenya, UN Agency Warns of Growing Humanitarian Needs Aquintero82/Wikimedia Commons A map showing the location of Kenya (in orange) and Ethiopia (in green). 30 October 2026 allAfrica.com By Peter Kenny Geneva — The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) says humanitarian needs are growing in an unfolding crisis on the Kenya–Ethiopia border as ongoing clashes on the Ethiopian side have forced tens of thousands of people to cross into Kenya in search of safety. Significant cross-border movements at Moyale have been reported since Oct. 22. “According to local authorities, up to an estimated 50,000 people have crossed into Kenya,” said Fatima Mohammed-Cole, the UNHCR Representative in Kenya. “The figure remains fluid as registration and verification efforts continue, amid reports of further crossings,” she said in a statement. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Many of those fleeing are women and children. The UN official said that while some affected people are staying with relatives and in host communities, others have sought shelter in temporary locations such as schools and churches. - FOOD: THE URGENT NEED “Food remains the most urgent need, alongside safe drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation and health care,” said Mohammed-Cole. UNHCR has deployed an emergency team to Moyale and is working closely with the Kenyan government. It is working alongside the UN migration agency, IOM; the UN children’s agency, UNICEF, the UN World Food Programme, the Kenya Red Cross Society, and other humanitarian partners, to support the national and local response. UNHCR said it is mobilising emergency relief supplies, including essential household items and temporary shelter materials, to support nearly 12,000 people, with efforts underway to increase assistance as needs grow. The agency is supporting ongoing assessments of protection and humanitarian needs. “We are also working with the authorities and partners to identify safer accommodation options, further away from the border, for those fleeing violence,” the UNHCR official said. According to Chatham House researchers, “Although Tigray has seen conflict before, this time there is a risk that hostilities could extend into Eritrea and Sudan,” they wrote . ethiopia.title: PM Abiy Invites Russian Institutions to Partner With Ethiopia's AI University
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Invites Russian Institutions to Partner With Ethiopia's AI University - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Invites Russian Institutions to Partner With Ethiopia's AI University 29 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has called for deeper scientific cooperation with Russia, specifically inviting Russian institutions to partner with Ethiopia's newly established Medemer University of Artificial Intelligence. Addressing the 3rd Russia-Africa Summit, the Prime Minister emphasized the importance of building local technological capabilities. "Ethiopia is establishing the Medemer University of Artificial Intelligence in Addis Ababa. We invite Russian universities and institutions to work with us in teaching and research." Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The initiative is part of Ethiopia's broader push for "technological sovereignty," ensuring that AI development reflects local needs. "An African researcher should be able to create tools in the language of our people, and our institutions should decide how those tools use our data," he said. Beyond AI, PM Abiy identified food security and energy as key pillars for cooperation, including the development of a nuclear power plant to diversify Ethiopia's energy mix. He stressed that these partnerships must focus on tangible outcomes. "Innovation must find its way into production and trade", the Premier noted. Reflecting on the historical ties between the two nations, which date back to the late 19th century, he emphasized that modern cooperation must be backed by clear action plans. The PM concluded by highlighting that true independence requires both the right to decide and the ability to execute those decisions. "Independence gives us a right to decide. Reflecting on the historical ties between Ethiopia and Russia, he called for modern collaborations to be supported by clear action plans, asserting that true independence involves both the right to make decisions and the capability to implement them.

Putin underscored Moscow's commitment to deepening economic and trade cooperation with Ethiopia. "I would like to highlight the substantial growth in bilateral trade, which exceeded 1.3 billion USD in January-September this year. This is more than double the figure for the whole of 2025," he said. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Speaking during talks with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on the sidelines of the Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on October 28, Putin said trade between the two countries had more than doubled the total recorded for the whole of 2025. He described Ethiopia-Russia relations as friendly and constructive, highlighting promising opportunities for large-scale cooperation in energy, agriculture, industry, peaceful space exploration, science, healthcare and education. "We have many promising large-scale projects across a wide range of areas, from energy, agriculture and industrial cooperation to the peaceful exploration of outer space, science, healthcare and education," he said. Putin reaffirmed Russia's commitment to deepening its longstanding relations with Ethiopia. He also described bilateral ties and his personal contacts with PM Abiy as friendly, substantive and constructive. He recalled their recent meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi in September, where the two leaders reviewed key areas of bilateral cooperation, according to the Russian Foreign Ministry. The Russian President also emphasized the countries' coordination on international affairs through the United Nations, BRICS and other multilateral forums. He said Russia fully supports Africa's emergence as one of the key centres of the emerging multipolar world order. President Putin added that Moscow would pay particular attention to expanding trade and economic cooperation with African countries, ensuring food and energy security, and developing healthcare. He further wished Ethiopia success in hosting the 2027 United Nations Climate Change Conference in Addis Ababa. He noted that the Third Russia-Africa Summit would conclude with the adoption of a declaration and a new Action Plan of the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum covering 2027-2029. The meeting, he said, provided an opportunity to continue discussions on strengthening the multifaceted relations between Ethiopia and Russia, alongside current regional and international issues. In an exclusive interview with ENA, Sylla commended Ethiopia's efforts to curb emissions through clean cooking, cleaner energy for vehicles, green corridors and large-scale tree planting, urging other African countries to learn from the experience and replicate the initiatives. Emphasizing the significance of leadership, he said "we can only commend the leadership of Ethiopia on those measures to curb emissions in the country, from clean cooking to cleaner energy for vehicles, all those green corridor as well with the goal of planting millions of trees in Ethiopia". The Director also stressed the need for African mayors and ministers of urban development to replicate Ethiopia's experience across the continent. Ethiopia has planted over 56 billion tree seedlings since the launching of the Green Legacy Initiative in 2019. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Commenting on the hosting of the 2027 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP) in Ethiopia, he said the event is an important opportunity for Africa to strengthen its voice in global climate negotiations, promote green investment, and demonstrate progress in addressing climate change. "We are all excited seeing Ethiopia hosting one of the most critical and most important COP in the human story." Sylla noted that the conference comes at a critical time and African countries could use the platform to highlight their climate initiatives, exchange experiences with other nations and strengthen cooperation in advancing the goals of the Paris Agreement. He underscored the importance of addressing climate change in Africa's rapidly urbanizing cities, noting that the continent faces growing needs for climate adaptation, mitigation and urban resilience. According to him, African cities require stronger measures to withstand the impacts of climate change. The UN-Habitat official emphasized that African countries and cities should strengthen solidarity, share knowledge and develop a common agenda that could be reflected in COP32's Action Agenda. Coordinated action among African countries would help advance urban climate solutions and enable cities to learn from one another's experiences, he added. Sylla further noted that UN-Habitat remains committed to supporting the Ethiopian government in ensuring the success of COP32. ethiopia.title: Ethiopian Arrivals Fleeing Moyale Conflict Into Northern Kenya Rise to Nearly 50,000 - 'Situation Remains Fluid': UN
ethiopia.content: Ethiopian Arrivals Fleeing Moyale Conflict Into Northern Kenya Rise to Nearly 50,000 - 'Situation Remains Fluid': UN - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopian Arrivals Fleeing Moyale Conflict Into Northern Kenya Rise to Nearly 50,000 - 'Situation Remains Fluid': UN UNFPA Kenya The ongoing drought and rising insecurity forced Rukia Yaarow Ali to leave her home in Somalia, to seek refuge in Daadab refugee complex in northern Kenya. 29 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Approximately 50,000 people have crossed from Ethiopia into northern Kenya following violent clashes around Moyale, with the International Organization for Migration (IOM) warning that further arrivals could overwhelm already strained local services and resources. "As of 29 October, an estimated 50,000 people had arrived in Moyale, Marsabit County," IOM said, adding that the arrivals were staying with local communities along the border, while others had sought shelter at five temporary sites. "Thousands of people have crossed into Kenya seeking safety, and most are being sheltered by local communities," said Nomagugu Ncube, IOM Kenya chief of mission. "The situation remains fluid, and the numbers of arrivals could increase in the coming days." Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines IOM said the immediate needs include water, shelter, healthcare, basic supplies, sanitation, and protection services. The agency said the Kenyan government and humanitarian partners are preparing a response targeting up to 80,000 people in anticipation of further arrivals. It is also supporting displacement assessments and planning emergency assistance, including shelter materials, essential household items, water tanks, and water purification tablets. The agency is working with the Kenyan government, the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), the Department of Refugee Services, and other humanitarian partners to monitor cross-border movements and identify priority needs. IOM cautioned that the arrival figures remain preliminary and could change as further information becomes available. The influx follows escalating conflict in Moyale , along the boundary between Ethiopia's Oromia and Somali regions, following a dispute over the raising of a Somali Regional State flag and the killing of 13-year-old Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa on October 18. Subsequent clashes between security forces from the two regions spread to seven districts, prompting civilian causalities, property destruction and residents to flee across the border. While some areas have reportedly experienced relative calm, the displacement continues to place pressure on host communities and humanitarian services in northern Kenya. somalia.title: Somalia Repatriates 169 from Libyan Prisons as Forced Removals from Europe Continue - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: Somalia Repatriates 169 from Libyan Prisons as Forced Removals from Europe Continue - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors International Relations Nationwide Somalia Repatriates 169 from Libyan Prisons as Forced Removals from Europe Continue October 30, 2026 6 min read MOGADISHU , The Federal Government of Somalia has repatriated 169 citizens who were held in prisons in Libya, with 140 arriving in Mogadishu and 29 flown to Hargeisa, according to a statement from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The return was carried out through the Voluntary Humanitarian Return programme, supported by the European Union in Somalia and implemented by the International Organization for Migration in coordination with the federal government. IOM described the operation as a “safe and dignified return” that gives the returnees a chance to reunite with their families and begin rebuilding their lives. Ibrahim Guure, director of the diaspora and communities department at the foreign ministry, was among the officials who received the returnees in Mogadishu. Separately, a debate on preventing youth irregular migration was held in Mogadishu, attended by Prof. Mohamed Omar Dhalxa and representatives of youth organizations. A Pattern of IOM-Supported Returns The operation is the latest in a series of repatriations that have become routine. In September 2026, 171 Somali migrants stranded in Libya were assisted to return home on an IOM charter flight, with 42 disembarking in Hargeisa and the remainder arriving in Mogadishu. As FTL Somalia reported , several of the migrants, including three minors, had endured dangerous travel conditions across multiple countries before encountering exploitation and abuse by smugglers in Libya. In July 2026, the National Commission for Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons provided immediate assistance to nearly 130 Somali nationals repatriated from Libyan detention centres, offering medical check-ups, registration with the National Identification and Registration Authority, and help reuniting with families. Earlier, in April 2026, 174 citizens were repatriated, with Deputy Foreign Minister Hassan Mohamed Ali welcoming them at Aden Adde International Airport. Since August 2022, the EU-funded Voluntary Humanitarian Return programme has facilitated the voluntary return of more than 2,000 Somali migrants from Libya, with additional charter flights expected in the final quarter of 2026. IOM has consistently stressed that every return under the programme is voluntary and based on the migrant’s informed decision, with counselling provided before departure and support framed around family reunification and dignity. The Contrast with Forced Removals The voluntary returns from Libya stand in contrast to the forced deportations Somalia has received from European countries. On the night of October 27-28, Sweden forcibly deported nine Somali nationals on a specially chartered aircraft, the latest in a series of removals that have drawn political scrutiny in Stockholm. As FTL Somalia reported , the deportation follows the case of Abas Bashir, a Somali father of six who appealed to President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud after alleging that three officials from the Office of the Prime Minister were involved in his forced removal. The Swedish government has acknowledged conditioning development assistance on Somalia’s willingness to accept deported nationals. Swedish media reported that approximately 100 million kronor in aid was redirected toward projects tied to the Prime Minister’s office, alongside five million kronor routed through the UN migration agency to fund three positions within the Somali government. The Somali government has described the allegations as “baseless and misleading,” while Swedish ministers have denied that funds reached the Prime Minister’s office directly. The financial architecture behind these returns remains contested. The allegations have not been independently investigated, and the Somali government’s denials, while categorical, do not address the specific claims made by Bashir or the Swedish media reports. What is clear is that the two streams of return operate under different logics: the Libya programme is EU-funded, voluntary, and framed around humanitarian protection and family reunification, while the Swedish removals are enforcement-driven and tied to the conditioning of development aid. The Drivers and the Debate The debate in Mogadishu on preventing irregular migration reflects a growing recognition that repatriation alone does not address why young Somalis embark on these journeys. Unemployment, limited economic opportunities, and insecurity continue to push youth toward irregular routes through Libya and the Mediterranean, where the risks of detention, exploitation, and death are well documented. IOM data shows that between January and March 2026 alone, 1,627 Somali migrants arrived in Libya through the Northern Route, and more than 1,500 were estimated to be stranded in the country as of July 2026, many living in dangerous conditions with limited access to food, shelter, and healthcare. The National Commission for Refugees and IDPs has begun enlisting young Somalis who survived migration journeys to warn others, gathering nearly 100 returnees in Mogadishu to share their experiences and establish a network for awareness campaigns. Critical Note The return of 169 citizens from Libyan prisons is a necessary intervention, and the coordination between the foreign ministry, the European Union, and IOM has made these operations possible. But the repetition of these flights, month after month, year after year, is itself the story that deserves more attention than any single repatriation. Each Voluntary Humanitarian Return represents lives pulled back from abuse and exploitation, and the programme’s emphasis on voluntariness, informed consent, and dignity is a meaningful distinction from the forced removals happening in Europe. Yet the flow of young Somalis toward Libya and the Mediterranean continues, driven by conditions at home that repatriation cannot fix. The debate in Mogadishu and the returnee-led awareness campaigns are welcome, but they operate at the level of warning and persuasion. They do not create jobs, do not improve security in the regions young people are leaving, and do not offer legal pathways abroad for those determined to go. The government’s focus on rescue operations is understandable, and its diplomatic engagement with Libyan authorities has secured the release of detainees. But a policy that is primarily reactive will keep producing the same scenes at Aden Adde airport: young people arriving with nothing, having survived a journey that many others did not. Meanwhile, the forced removals from Sweden raise questions about the financial arrangements underpinning returns cooperation that the government has not fully answered. Until the economic and security conditions that push young people onto these routes change, and until the transparency of forced returns is addressed, the repatriation flights will continue to be necessary, and the debate in Mogadishu will remain a conversation about symptoms rather than causes. Speaking in an interview with Sky News on Oct. 30, Hassan Sheikh said Somalia was not a party to the disagreements between Addis Ababa and Asmara and had no intention of taking sides. advertisements “We have good relations with Ethiopia, and we also have good relations with Eritrea. Whatever occurs between the two countries is a matter for them alone; we are not a part of it, and there are no conflicts in which we seek to intervene,” the president said. Hassan Sheikh emphasized that Somalia's foreign policy is guided by peaceful coexistence, mutual understanding and cooperation with neighboring countries. He said the government's priority was to maintain stability at home while fostering constructive relations with other countries. The president described Somalia's guiding principle as being at peace with itself and with the rest of the world, stressing that Mogadishu does not seek involvement in conflicts between other nations. His remarks come amid renewed diplomatic and political tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea, raising concerns about the potential consequences for security and stability across the Horn of Africa. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara have deteriorated amid disagreements over regional security and competing political interests. Somalia maintains diplomatic relations with both countries and has emphasized the importance of dialogue and cooperation in addressing regional disputes. somalia.content: Somalia and the ‘Bilateralisation’ of the War Against Al-Shabaab and ISIS - Realnews Magazine 30th Oct, 2026 POLITICS OIL & GAS BUSINESS ENVIRONMENT WOMEN YOUTH EDUCATION AFRICA ADVERT RATES Advert Rates 🡢 Contact Us 🡢 Events 🡢 Photo Gallery 🡢 Realnews TV 🡢 Vision and Mission 🡢 Somalia and the ‘Bilateralisation’ of the War Against Al-Shabaab and ISIS Fri, Oct 30, 2026 By editor 4 MIN READ Opinion SOMALIA’s campaign against Al-Shabaab is increasingly characterised by bilateral troop deployments, Somali-led ground operations and external military support. This model offers tactical advantages, but questions remain over coordination, sustainability and the future role of the African Union mission. Recent operations in Somalia’s Lower Shabelle, together with an increased tempo of US airstrikes, highlight the growing importance of bilateral military arrangements alongside the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM). In March 2026, Somali National Army forces, supported by AUSSOM’s Ugandan contingent and international partners, announced the recapture of Mubarak and Daarusalaam in Lower Shabelle. Subsequent operations in April targeted additional insurgent positions, with AUSSOM reporting air cover and coordinated ground action. These operations demonstrate the continuing importance of cooperation between Somali forces, AU contingents and external partners. The United States has maintained a significant counterterrorism air campaign. On 17 October, US Africa Command (AFRICOM) confirmed an airstrike targeting Al-Shabaab near Dhooble Airport in southern Somalia. AFRICOM’s published register recorded 88 strikes in Somalia during 2026 at the time of writing, targeting both Al-Shabaab and ISIS-Somalia. This illustrates the scale of US involvement, although it does not establish that American air assets supported every successful ground operation. Türkiye has also expanded its military engagement with Somalia through training, defence cooperation and the deployment of F-16 fighter aircraft, publicly demonstrated in April 2026. However, their presence does not establish that Turkish combat aircraft supported the specific operations in Lower Shabelle. Bilateral troop deployments represent another significant development. According to The EastAfrican , Uganda is assessed to have between 4,000 and 6,000 troops deployed under bilateral arrangements, in addition to its allocated AUSSOM contingent of approximately 4,500. Ethiopia is also reported to have around 5,000 bilateral troops in Somalia, alongside its 2,500-person AU allocation. These figures are estimates rather than independently verified totals. The distinction matters. AUSSOM provides a multilateral framework for supporting stabilisation and Somali security forces. Bilateral deployments operate through national arrangements with the Somali government. Although they may complement the AU mission, their command relationships, operational priorities and support arrangements are not necessarily identical. This emerging pattern has been described as the ‘ bilateralisation’ of the war against Al-Shabaab. It suggests a shift towards national troop deployments and direct military assistance operating alongside the formal AU framework. International involvement extends beyond conventional military support. Photographs reported by The EastAfrican following operations in Lower Shabelle showed Somali and Ugandan troops alongside personnel from Bancroft Global Development, a contractor involved in training and mentoring Somali forces. Its presence illustrates the proximity of specialist support to frontline operations, although it does not establish a combat role. The operational advantages of this model are apparent. Bilateral forces can supplement available manpower, while air support can disrupt insurgent positions and create opportunities for ground forces to advance. Intelligence, training and logistics can further improve operational effectiveness. Recent successes suggest these elements can be mutually reinforcing when effectively coordinated. Nevertheless, the precise relationship between bilateral deployments, US strikes and Turkish military activity requires further evidence. The presence of several international partners does not establish a joint command structure, nor does the timing of airstrikes and ground advances prove direct causation. There are also strategic risks. Reliance on external air power and foreign troops may produce tactical gains without delivering lasting security. Holding recovered territory requires secure supply routes, capable Somali forces, functioning local administration and sufficient public confidence to prevent insurgents from returning. AUSSOM’s future remains central to this debate. Its authorised strength must be distinguished from the number of troops actually deployed and available for operations. Egypt’s participation was already being prepared in February 2026; any further expansion should be assessed against confirmed decisions rather than reported proposals. The central question is not whether bilateral deployments should replace multilateral cooperation, but how they can reinforce a coherent, Somali-led security strategy. Greater operational flexibility and external support may generate battlefield gains, but their longer-term value will depend on whether those gains endure, coordination remains effective and Somali institutions can assume lasting responsibility for security. The experience of 2026 points to the growing importance of bilateral military arrangements in Somalia’s campaign against Al-Shabaab and ISIS-Somalia. The model has potential, but tactical success should not be confused with strategic victory. Its ultimate test is whether international support builds sustainable Somali security capabilities rather than enduring dependence on external forces. somalia.content: "Not Under Any Circumstances": Somalia's President Draws a Red Line on Foreign Bases and Israeli Presence - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors International Relations Nationwide “Not Under Any Circumstances”: Somalia’s President Draws a Red Line on Foreign Bases and Israeli Presence October 30, 2026 5 min read MOGADISHU , President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has said his government will not permit foreign countries to establish military bases in Somalia for their own geopolitical purposes, drawing a clear line amid intensifying competition over the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa. In an interview with Sky News, Mohamud said Somalia would not give any country the opportunity to set up bases inside the country to pursue its own interests. The remarks came in response to questions about the activities of countries including Russia, Israel, Türkiye, the United States, and Ethiopia in the region. The President also addressed Somalia’s relationship with the United Arab Emirates, confirming that the defense and security agreements signed with Abu Dhabi had been cancelled. He said the UAE’s activities inside Somalia no longer rest on a valid legal agreement. In the same interview, Mohamud was asked about Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro’s recent visit to Washington. He downplayed its significance, saying that anyone can travel to the United States, obtain a visa, stay for a period of time and build friendships there. He said the US government has consistently respected Somalia’s unity and thanked Washington for that position. The UAE Rupture and Its Legal Basis The cancellation of the UAE agreements was first announced in January 2026, when the federal government annulled all agreements with Abu Dhabi, including those covering ports, security, and defense. Defense Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi said at the time that the decision was based on “reliable reports and evidence indicating practices linked to the United Arab Emirates that undermine the sovereignty of the Somali Republic, its national unity and political independence.” The dispute centered in part on the UAE’s long-standing economic and security ties with Somaliland, including its involvement in the port of Berbera. Mogadishu objected to arrangements it considered to bypass the federal government. President Mohamud later said Somalia remained open to repairing relations with Abu Dhabi, noting that diplomatic channels had not been severed, but that the agreements themselves had been cancelled. DP World, the Emirati logistics giant that invested approximately $442 million in Berbera Port, confirmed that its operations there would continue under existing agreements , defying Mogadishu’s annulment. The Israeli Dimension The President’s remarks on foreign bases come amid heightened scrutiny of Israeli activities in the region. In a separate interview with Al Jazeera in early October, Mohamud said Israel planned to establish a naval base in Berbera and use the city’s airport, describing Israel’s recognition of Somaliland as an “existential threat” to Somalia’s unity. He said attempts to pull Somalia into the Middle East’s crises would not succeed. Somaliland rejected Mohamud’s claims in a formal statement, asserting that Mogadishu has no authority over its foreign relations and defending its ties with Israel as “the sovereign decisions of two states.” As FTL Somalia reported , the statement did not address questions about the involvement of Israeli infrastructure companies with records of settlement construction in the occupied West Bank. The President’s Sky News interview reinforced that position, framing the rejection of foreign proxy bases as a matter of national sovereignty. The Regional Context Somalia’s stance unfolds against a backdrop of escalating competition in the Red Sea and Horn of Africa. Türkiye maintains its largest overseas military base in Mogadishu and has deepened its economic and security footprint, including a hydrocarbon exploration agreement that critics have described as lopsided. The United States operates a base at Balidogle and has maintained security cooperation with Mogadishu, while the UAE has established facilities in Bosaso, Berbera, and previously in Kismayo. Somaliland officials have said their diplomatic normalization with Israel was motivated in part by the need to counter Turkey’s military footprint in Somalia, with Hargeisa seeking Israeli air defense systems to offset Turkish drones and warplanes deployed in Mogadishu, as FTL Somalia reported . The presence of multiple foreign military facilities in Somalia and its surroundings has made the question of basing rights a sensitive political issue. President Mohamud’s statement appears designed to assert federal authority over any future arrangements, and to signal that Somalia will not be used as a staging ground in conflicts it does not control. Critical Note President Mohamud’s statement is a clear assertion of sovereignty, but it sits uneasily with the reality of Somalia’s security dependency. The country hosts foreign forces under the AUSSOM mandate and bilateral agreements, and it relies on external partners for training, equipment, and logistics. The line between a “base” and a “training facility” or “logistics hub” is not always clear, and the government’s own security arrangements with Türkiye and the United States involve a permanent foreign military presence. The rejection of proxy bases is therefore less a description of current reality than a declaration of intent about future arrangements. It is aimed at preventing Somalia from becoming a pawn in the rivalry between Israel, Türkiye, and the Gulf states, a rivalry that has already drawn Somaliland into its orbit through Israel’s recognition and the UAE’s port investments. Whether the President can maintain that position will depend on his government’s ability to balance its security partnerships. Türkiye is Somalia’s most important military partner, and its presence is not likely to be described as a “proxy base.” The United States maintains its own facility. The UAE has been pushed out, at least formally. The question is whether other partners will accept the same terms, or whether Somalia’s need for security will eventually force it to accept arrangements it has publicly ruled out. The approvals, made at the Fund’s 47th Board meeting on 23 October 2026, include a five-year, US$30 million programme across the Mandera Triangle of the Horn of Africa and a separate US$4.97 million project targeting smallholder farmers in Eastern Rwanda . The funding forms part of US$98.8 million in new project approvals announced by the Adaptation Fund in October. Its allocation to the four African countries reflects growing attention to adaptation investments that address immediate climate vulnerabilities while protecting agricultural production, water resources and livelihoods. Unlike mitigation projects focused primarily on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, the programmes are designed to help communities and institutions manage the effects of climate change that are already disrupting economic activity. The largest allocation will support communities across Kenya’s Mandera County , Somalia’s Gedo Region and Ethiopia’s Liben and Afder zones. The area, commonly referred to as the Mandera Triangle , faces recurring droughts and floods that affect pastoralist and agro-pastoralist livelihoods, strain water resources and disrupt the movement of people and livestock across national borders. According to FurtherAfrica , the US$30 million programme will be implemented over five years by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) , working alongside the Intergovernmental Authority on Development’s climate adaptation centre and the three participating governments. It aims to reach 500,000 people directly and a further 1.2 million indirectly through improved early warning systems and safer cross-border movement. The programme will restore degraded rangelands, improve water systems and expand income-generating opportunities for women and pastoralist communities. It will also strengthen coordination between communities and public institutions so that warnings of droughts, floods and other climate hazards can inform timely responses across the border region. The cross border design is significant because climate risks in the Horn of Africa do not follow national boundaries. Pastoralist communities depend on seasonal access to grazing land and water sources that may extend across several countries. Drought in one area can increase pressure on resources elsewhere, while flooding can disrupt transport routes, trade and the movement of livestock. National adaptation programmes operating independently may therefore struggle to address risks that are shared across an interconnected ecological and economic system. For Kenya , the programme has direct implications for Mandera County , where recurrent water shortages and pressure on pastoralist livelihoods can affect household incomes, livestock productivity and local markets. Investments in water infrastructure and rangeland restoration could help reduce losses during periods of climate stress, although their long-term value will depend on maintenance, equitable access and effective management of shared resources. The programme also places regional institutions at the centre of adaptation delivery. IGAD has a mandate to coordinate responses to climate and development challenges across the Horn of Africa , where environmental pressures intersect with displacement, food insecurity and cross-border economic activity. Strengthening early warning systems and cooperation between national authorities could improve the ability of governments to prepare for climate shocks before they escalate into humanitarian and economic crises. Rwanda will receive US$4.97 million for a separate four-year programme targeting at least 10,000 smallholder farmers in Kayonza , Gatsibo and Nyagatare districts. The project will be implemented by Rwanda’s Ministry of Agriculture and Animal Resources with support from UNDP , while farmer cooperatives and local authorities will contribute to adaptation planning. The Rwanda programme will expand farmers’ access to seasonal weather forecasts and promote climate-smart agricultural practices. Better climate information can help farmers make decisions about planting periods, crop management and the use of available water, reducing the uncertainty associated with changing rainfall patterns. For smallholder households whose incomes depend heavily on agricultural production, the timing and reliability of such information can influence both harvest outcomes and food security. Read also: https://furtherafrica.com/2026/10/29/adaptation-fund-backs-africa-climate-resilience-with-us35m/ Agriculture remains an important source of employment and income across the region, but its dependence on rainfall leaves farmers exposed to increasingly variable weather conditions. When drought or irregular rainfall reduces yields, the consequences extend beyond individual farms to food prices, household purchasing power and the supply of agricultural products to domestic markets. Investments in climate information, water management and more resilient production systems can therefore support wider economic stability. The two programmes also illustrate different approaches to adaptation finance. The Mandera Triangle project focuses on shared ecosystems, water resources and cross-border pastoralist systems, while Rwanda’s allocation concentrates on agricultural resilience at district and farm level. Both rely on local institutions and community participation, recognising that adaptation measures are more likely to be effective when they reflect the conditions and priorities of the people expected to use them. However, approval of funding does not guarantee that intended outcomes will be achieved. Implementation will depend on the timely release and management of resources, coordination between governments and delivery partners, procurement capacity and the ability to maintain infrastructure after project funding ends. In the Mandera Triangle , cooperation across three countries will be particularly important, given differences in public institutions, security conditions and local resource-management arrangements. Measuring results will also be essential. The number of people reached provides an indication of programme scale, but longer-term performance will depend on whether water systems remain functional, early warnings reach communities in time, rangelands recover and farmers adopt practices that improve resilience. Transparent reporting on expenditure, delivery milestones and the distribution of benefits will help determine whether the funding translates into lasting improvements. The approvals come as African governments face growing pressure to finance adaptation while managing debt obligations, infrastructure deficits and competing public spending priorities. International climate funds can provide resources for projects that may struggle to attract commercial investment, particularly where benefits such as reduced disaster losses, improved food security and stronger ecosystem management do not generate direct financial returns. Their effectiveness, however, depends on whether funding reaches vulnerable communities and strengthens the institutions responsible for sustaining the investments. For the Horn of Africa , where droughts and floods can affect livestock markets, agricultural production, water access and regional mobility, the programme places climate resilience within a broader development and economic security agenda. In Rwanda , the focus on smallholder farmers connects adaptation directly to agricultural productivity and food system stability. The nearly US$35 million approval provides financing for two distinct but related adaptation challenges. Its longer-term significance will depend on whether the programmes strengthen the systems communities rely on to manage climate shocks, from shared water resources and regional early warning networks to farm level decisions that protect production and household incomes. This funding, announced during the Fund's 47th Board meeting on October 23, 2026, includes a $30 million program for the Mandera Triangle, which encompasses parts of Kenya, Somalia, and Ethiopia, and a $4.97 million project for smallholder farmers in Rwanda. The Mandera Triangle project aims to assist 500,000 people directly and 1.2 million indirectly by enhancing water systems and improving cross-border cooperation in response to climate hazards. In Rwanda, the initiative will support 10,000 farmers by providing access to weather forecasts and promoting sustainable agricultural practices. These programs highlight the importance of local institutions and community involvement in adaptation efforts, addressing immediate climate vulnerabilities while aiming for long-term resilience in the face of increasing climate variability.
