It has a Foreign Investment Law, an Investors and Investments Protection Law, and a new Investment Law enacted in 2025 that established the Somalia Investment Promotion Agency and a National Investment Council, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the new investment law . It has a National Investment Promotion Strategy and a “one-stop shop” registration system. Its officials travel to Gulf capitals and European forums to present Somalia as “open for business.” But the 2026 Investment Climate Statement, published by the U.S. Department of State, paints a more complicated picture. While the legal framework for investment has expanded, the institutions needed to enforce it have not kept pace. The report identifies a series of structural barriers that continue to deter the very capital the government is trying to attract: a judicial system incapable of resolving commercial disputes, weak property rights, rampant corruption, a financial sector cut off from the global system, and an insurgency that taxes businesses with impunity. The Laws Exist. The Courts Do Not. The report notes that Somalia has no commercial courts. Domestic court processes are “widely viewed as corrupt and subject to external interference.” A 2020 USAID-funded report found that the courts lack political independence and face competition from parallel Al-Shabaab -run Islamic courts, which some citizens reportedly use because they are perceived as more efficient and less corrupt than the formal system. For foreign investors, this is a fundamental problem. A contract is only as valuable as the ability to enforce it. The report states that “weak judicial capacity, limited administrative law procedures, corruption concerns, and inconsistent enforcement reduce the effectiveness and predictability of judicial review.” As a result, investors often rely on clan mediation or international arbitration outside Somalia, typically in Djibouti or the UAE. The government has announced plans to establish a commercial court system in 2026, but no such courts currently exist. And while the 2023 Investors and Investments Protection Law provides for arbitration under international rules, Somalia is not a party to the New York Convention, meaning foreign arbitral awards are not automatically enforceable in Somali courts. The Financial Chokehold Somalia’s investment climate cannot be separated from its financial isolation. The State Department report notes that “moving money into and around the country through traditional banking mechanisms is difficult,” and that the financial sector is constrained by a lack of correspondent banking relationships. The cost of this isolation is measurable. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the financial sector , Central Bank Governor Abdirahman M. Abdullahi has estimated that Somalia loses approximately $210 million annually to intermediary fees because no Somali bank can send or receive U.S. dollars directly. Every transaction is routed through correspondent institutions in other countries, adding cost and opacity at each step. The State Department identifies the root cause: concerns that Al-Shabaab and ISIS-Somalia exploit regulatory and legal deficiencies in the financial sector. These gaps include weak Know Your Customer capabilities, incomplete anti-money laundering laws, and limited use of national identification documents. The Central Bank has licensed 15 commercial banks and six mobile money providers, but correspondent relationships remain limited to partial arrangements with institutions in Türkiye, Kenya, and the UAE. The Gap Between Promotion and Investment The government’s investment promotion efforts are active, but they often run ahead of the conditions needed to sustain the investments they seek. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Egyptian-backed Zain-al-Abdin Group’s visit , the Director General of the Investment Promotion Agency, Faisal Adam Hassan, received a delegation from the company to discuss potential investments in fisheries, agriculture, and livestock. The visit is part of a sustained effort to attract international capital to a sector the government estimates could generate billions of dollars annually. But as FTL Somalia noted, the sectors being pitched are precisely those where the state’s ability to protect and regulate is weakest. An Egyptian investor exploring fisheries opportunities will find a coastline rich in fish and poor in the infrastructure needed to extract value from it. The SomTürk precedent, which has already provoked a formal rejection from Puntland, illustrates the risk that any major fisheries deal will become entangled in the federal-state dispute. An investor considering a multi-year commitment would be prudent to ask which authority will regulate their license, protect their assets, and honor their contract in three years’ time. The government’s investment promotion agency can facilitate meetings and provide information. It cannot guarantee that the courts will enforce a contract or that a regional administration will recognize a federal concession. The $2 Billion Lifeline the State Cannot Fully Control Remittances remain the backbone of Somalia’s economy, estimated at roughly $2 billion annually, or about 25 percent of GDP. Most inflows are processed through hawalas and mobile money platforms, which have become the primary channel for household income, food, education, and small business investment. The State Department report details how the government is trying to regulate this sector to counter terrorist financing. The National Anti-Money Laundering Committee has issued guidelines to mobile money operators limiting daily transactions per account to $300 and requiring biometric registration of customers. The Central Bank has launched the Somali Payment Switch and the Somali Instant Payment System to enable real-time, interoperable payments. But the tension is inherent. As FTL Somalia reported in its coverage of the financial sector, the reforms are real but the trust deficit persists. International donors and financial institutions have been shaken by repeated allegations of aid diversion and corruption, and the burden of proof remains on Somali institutions to show that the billions flowing into the country are reaching those who need them most. The Security Tax The State Department report is blunt about the security environment. Al-Shabaab “controls large parts of south-central Somalia and conducts attacks on government facilities, civilians, and business.” The group “routinely extorts payments from businesses and households.” Insecurity is “frequently cited by businesses as the top constraint to operating in Somalia.” This is not an abstract threat. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of counter-extortion operations , Somali security forces have conducted repeated raids on Al-Shabaab checkpoints and “tax collectors,” seizing extortion receipts and dismantling the group’s revenue infrastructure. The group has long relied on illegal taxation of civilians, businesses, and road users as a primary source of funding, collecting an estimated $120 million annually from farmers, traders, and vulnerable rural communities, as detailed in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the group’s revenue networks . For investors, this means accounting for additional costs: restricted movement, insurance, personnel and facility protection, and in some cases, payments to both the government and the insurgency. The State Department also notes a “general risk of wrongful detention” due to fragmented legal frameworks governing judicial and police processes. The New Investment Architecture and Its Limits The government has not been idle. The 2025 Investment Law, approved by the Senate in November 2025, established the Somalia Investment Promotion Agency as the central investment facilitation agency under the Ministry of Planning, Investment and Economic Development, with a mandate to streamline procedures and provide one-stop-shop services. In May 2025, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud signed four economic reform bills into law: the Insurance (Takaful) Bill, the Income Tax Bill, the Revised Financial Institutions Bill, and the Revised Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Bill. The President described them as “transformative tools” to bolster investor confidence and protect financial systems, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the reform bills . But the State Department report notes that “implementation remains at an early stage, and institutional capacity constraints persist.” The National Investment Incentives Framework, initiated in 2024 to formalize tax holidays and customs exemptions, remains in draft form. Investment incentives continue to be applied on an ad hoc basis, with line ministers and the Prime Minister offering discretionary exemptions. Critical Note The State Department’s report is not an investment promotion brochure. It is a risk assessment, and its findings are a useful corrective to the government’s optimistic narrative. Somalia has made real progress in passing investment laws. The 2023 Investors and Investments Protection Law, the 2025 Investment Law, and the establishment of the investment promotion agency provide a legal framework that did not exist a decade ago. The creation of a one-stop shop and the signing of financial reform bills signal intent. But laws are not institutions. A commercial code is meaningless without commercial courts. An investment protection law is hollow without a functioning land registry. A tax incentive framework is ineffective when incentives are granted through discretionary deals between ministers and investors. The financial isolation is perhaps the most binding constraint. The State Department notes that the lack of correspondent banking is rooted in AML/CFT concerns, but the government’s reforms, while real, have not yet convinced international banks to reconnect. The $210 million annual loss to intermediary fees is a direct cost of this trust deficit, and it falls hardest on the remittances that sustain ordinary households. The security tax is the other unavoidable reality. Al-Shabaab’s extortion networks are not a peripheral nuisance. They are a parallel fiscal system that competes with the state, and they operate in the same territory where the government is trying to attract investment. The counter-extortion operations that FTL Somalia has documented are necessary, but they are not sufficient to create the predictability that long-term capital requires. The government’s stated goal is to attract $5.3 billion in private investment under the National Transformation Plan. That is an ambitious target for any country, let alone one with an active insurgency and a judicial system that cannot enforce contracts. The report suggests that the government’s priority should be less on passing new laws and more on building the institutions that make existing laws work. Until that happens, Somalia will remain open for business in name, but closed for justice in practice. The announcement follows a meeting on Oct. 24 between the commander of the Turkish Land Forces and his Somali counterpart, who was accompanied by a military delegation. According to the Turkish Defence Ministry, the discussions focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation in defence, military training and security. Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to continuing military cooperation aimed at improving the capabilities of Somalia’s armed forces and contributing to regional security and stability. Turkey is one of Somalia’s key military partners, providing training, equipment and technical assistance to Somali security forces. Ankara operates a major military training facility in Mogadishu, where Turkish instructors have trained Somali soldiers as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s defence capabilities. The two countries have also expanded their military relationship through defence and maritime security agreements aimed at improving Somalia’s capacity to protect its territorial waters and combat security threats. The planned deployment of the two warships comes as Somalia and Turkey continue to deepen their military partnership, including cooperation on training, maritime security and defence capacity-building. somalia.title: The 4.5 Formula Meets the Payroll: How Clan Power-Sharing Undermines Meritocracy - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: The 4.5 Formula Meets the Payroll: How Clan Power-Sharing Undermines Meritocracy - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Politics Nationwide The 4.5 Formula Meets the Payroll: How Clan Power-Sharing Undermines Meritocracy October 30, 2026 8 min read MOGADISHU , Somalia’s civilian public administration is small by international standards, but it consumes a disproportionate share of the country’s limited fiscal resources. The civilian wage bill, excluding security forces, was estimated at 2.4 percent of GDP in 2024, or roughly 20 percent of total government expenditure. The federal government alone spent 1.3 percent of GDP on civilian wages, representing 17 percent of its total spending, according to the World Bank’s 2026 Public Finance Review. The figures reveal a paradox. Somalia has fewer civil servants per capita than most post-conflict peers, yet the wage bill absorbs a large share of domestic revenue because the revenue base is so narrow. The World Bank notes that this crowding-out effect leaves non-wage operational and service delivery expenditures underfunded, constraining the effectiveness of public institutions. The One-in-Four Problem The most striking feature of Somalia’s civil service is not its size, but its fragmentation. Only about one in four employees at the federal level, and one in five at the state level, is a formal civil servant, subject to established legal frameworks, pay scales, and payroll processing through the government’s financial management system. The remaining workforce operates under temporary, project-funded, or externally financed arrangements, often outside standardized human resource systems. This hybrid structure blurs accountability, weakens workforce planning, and reduces transparency in compensation practices. It also makes it difficult to determine the true size, cost, and function of the public sector. As the World Bank notes, a significant number of public employees, including teachers, health workers, and project staff, remain outside the formal civil service envelope. In 2024, project-financed and non-project advisory positions exceeded formal federal civil service posts by about 26 percent. The consequences are fiscal and institutional. When projects wind down, the government cannot absorb these positions at current pay and staffing levels without an unsustainable expansion of recurrent spending. The World Bank warns that this creates a choice between abrupt disruptions in service delivery and an unaffordable wage bill. The Meritocracy Battle: A Reform Blocked The fragmentation of the civil service is compounded by the political economy in which it operates, and by a reform agenda that has collided with parliamentary resistance. In September 2026, Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre issued a directive requiring all government ministries and agencies to implement merit-based recruitment and appointments, citing Article 161(1) of the Constitution and the Civil Service Law, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Prime Minister’s call for a merit-driven society . The Prime Minister described directors general as the backbone of state administration and said the purpose was to establish a professional and permanent administrative leadership capable of implementing government policy. The National Civil Service Commission (NCSC) followed with a directive implementing the order, signed by Commission Chairperson Mohamed Bashiir Ali. The directive established that all Director General positions would be filled through internal merit-based recruitment, with vacant positions filled through open competition. It included a special note emphasizing that women working in government ministries who meet the requirements should be given priority. But the reform was blocked. On September 22, 2026, the House of the People voted 136 to revoke the proposed civil service regulations, dealing a significant blow to the plan. The parliamentary vote followed a challenge from the House Committee on Social Services Development, chaired by MP Nadra Salah Abdi, which argued that the existing Civil Service Commission, composed of 14 members under a 2006 law, does not comply with Article 158(3) of the Constitution, which requires 15 members. The committee also challenged a 2023 resolution that transferred recruitment powers to the Prime Minister’s Office, stating that it contravenes the Constitution and the Commission’s authority, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the parliamentary block . The dispute exposed conflicting positions within the government itself. Deputy Prime Minister Salah Jama had previously described the Civil Service Commission as the “backbone of the government’s administrative system,” emphasizing its role in ensuring transparency, efficiency, and professionalism, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Deputy Prime Minister’s visit to the Commission . Yet Parliament, citing constitutional technicalities, blocked the very reform the Commission was tasked to implement. The practical effect is visible in the appointments themselves. In September 2026, Prime Minister Barre appointed new Directors General for the Ministries of Energy and Communications, citing the need to accelerate government operations, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the appointments . The statement did not clarify whether these appointments were made through the competitive process the Prime Minister had mandated, or through direct appointment. The ambiguity is telling: the reform was announced, the process was blocked, and the appointments continued. The 4.5 Formula and the Meritocracy Deficit The fragmentation of the civil service is further compounded by the 4.5 clan power-sharing formula. Established as a transitional mechanism in the 1990s and formalized through successive political agreements, the formula divides representation among major clan families and has been extended into the allocation of public positions, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the 4.5 system’s origins . The World Bank does not directly attribute the wage bill’s inefficiencies to the 4.5 formula, but its analysis of recruitment and career management points to governance and political economy constraints that limit meritocracy. The Heritage Institute has found that nearly one-quarter of appointments occur outside open competition, while 73 percent of respondents reported challenges during recruitment. Temporary recruitment channels allow senior officials to make direct appointments without vacancy notices, job descriptions, or standardized pay, increasing risks of nepotism, patronage, and political influence. The result is a system in which qualifications, experience, and performance are often secondary to clan affiliation and political loyalty. The World Bank describes this as a factor that “reduces the effectiveness of the formal civil service and increases reliance on temporary staff and consultants to perform core functions.” This duplication raises recurrent costs without commensurate improvements in service delivery. The government has acknowledged the problem. A new Pay and Grading Policy was approved by the Cabinet in December 2022, and the World Bank’s Somalia Enhancing Public Resource Management Project is supporting a comprehensive job analysis across approximately 63 ministries, departments, and agencies, covering a workforce of around 20,000 employees. The objective is to develop a logical and consistent job classification system aligned with the new policy. But the reform faces a fundamental obstacle. As the World Bank notes, the adoption of sensitive civil service reforms takes time, and it requires identifying reform champions who can expedite the process. In a system where appointment and promotion are shaped by clan and political calculations, the technical work of job evaluation is necessary but not sufficient. Without a political commitment to merit-based recruitment, the new pay and grading system risks becoming another layer of formalism on top of a patronage structure. Critical Note The World Bank’s findings describe a civil service that is caught between two imperatives. It must be small enough to be affordable, given Somalia’s narrow revenue base, but it must also be capable enough to deliver the services that citizens expect and that state-building requires. The current system achieves neither. It is fragmented, with a large share of its workforce outside formal structures, and it is costly, with a wage bill that crowds out the operational spending needed to make those workers effective. The 4.5 formula is often defended as a necessary stabilizer in a divided society. That defense has merit. But the formula was designed to allocate political representation, not to govern the recruitment and promotion of teachers, health workers, and civil servants. When it extends into the civil service, it becomes a mechanism for patronage rather than a safeguard against exclusion. The result is a bureaucracy that reflects clan balances rather than professional competence, and a wage bill that pays for positions rather than performance. The parliamentary block on the Prime Minister’s merit-based hiring directive complicates the picture further. The committee’s objections were framed in constitutional terms, but the effect was to preserve a system in which direct appointments remain possible. The Prime Minister’s subsequent appointments of Directors General, without public clarification of whether they followed the competitive process he mandated, suggest that the reform remains contested and incompletely implemented. A civil service can be inclusive without being captured. The question is whether Somalia’s leaders are prepared to make that distinction, or whether the 4.5 formula will continue to define not just who sits in parliament, but who teaches in classrooms and who manages the ministries.
